title: RFID Manufacturer for Brazil — Factory-Direct China
summary: Proud Tek ships RFID to Brazil factory-direct from Shenzhen with Brazil-market spec sheets. The one fact that decides a UHF order: Brazil runs two sub-bands — 902-907.5 MHz and 915-928 MHz, with a cellular guard gap at 907.5-915 MHz — under ANATEL restricted-radiation rules, so a reader set to the full 902-928 MHz band is non-compliant. Passive inlays are tuned for the Brazilian bands, and the reader — not the passive tag — carries ANATEL homologation. Access cards run at 13.56 MHz (HF), which is global. Express air reaches Guarulhos, Galeao and Viracopos in 7-10 business days; there is no China-Brazil free trade agreement, so import taxes (II, IPI, PIS/COFINS and state ICMS) are settled by the importer of record via SISCOMEX — we quote EXW/FOB/CIF, put the NCM on every invoice, and work with your Brazilian broker.

Built for Brazil's applications: retail item-level UHF, livestock ear tags (UHF plus LF 134.2 kHz, ISO 11784/11785 for the world's largest cattle herd), toll/ETC windshield stickers, logistics, and MIFARE and NFC cards.

Landed honestly — no China-Brazil FTA, so II/IPI/PIS-COFINS/ICMS are paid at clearance by the importer of record via SISCOMEX; we quote EXW/FOB/CIF, provide NCM guidance, and work with your customs broker (7-10 days air, 25-35 days sea).

sections.title: Get the band right: 902-907.5 MHz + 915-928 MHz under ANATEL
sections.intro: The single most expensive mistake in cross-border RFID sourcing is band mismatch — and Brazil is the trickiest UHF market to get right. It does not use one clean block like the US 902-928 MHz; it carves out two sub-bands, 902-907.5 MHz and 915-928 MHz, and leaves a guard gap at 907.5-915 MHz to protect the cellular band. A reader set to the full 902-928 MHz range is operating illegally in Brazil. New to frequency planning? Start with our [LF vs HF vs UHF guide](/blog/rfid-frequencies-lf-hf-uhf-explained/). Order the Brazilian sub-band tuning on the PO; access cards at 13.56 MHz are global and unaffected.

sections.title: Landed cost: NCM 8523.52, no FTA, and Brazil's cumulative tax stack
sections.intro: The unit price is the headline; in Brazil the landed cost is a whole chapter. Brazil has no free trade agreement with China, so there is no tariff preference to claim — instead there is a cumulative stack of import taxes settled at customs. Our [RFID RFP template](/blog/rfid-rfp-template-questions-suppliers/) shows the quote-comparison math; the Brazil-specific short version is below. RFID cards and tags classify under NCM 8523.52 (the Mercosur nomenclature aligned to HS 8523.52). Because there is no China-Brazil free trade agreement, there is no duty preference: the Import Duty (II) applies on the CIF value, then the IPI, PIS/COFINS and the state-level ICMS are layered on cumulatively, so the effective uplift on the CIF value is significant and varies by NCM and by the destination state's ICMS rate. Brazilian import taxes are paid by the importer of record when the goods clear through SISCOMEX, which is why we quote EXW, FOB or CIF and provide NCM guidance rather than a folded-in DDP number — your customs broker files the Import Declaration (DI) and settles the taxes. Confirm the exact rates for your NCM and state with your broker before you commit. (Sources: US Dept of Commerce — Brazil Country Commercial Guide (Import Tariffs); ANATEL.)

faq.question: Which UHF band do your tags use for Brazil?
faq.answer: Brazil authorises UHF RFID only in two sub-bands — 902-907.5 MHz and 915-928 MHz — with a guard gap at 907.5-915 MHz that protects the cellular band, under ANATEL's restricted-radiation rules (up to 4 W EIRP with frequency hopping). We tune passive inlays for those Brazilian sub-bands. A reader set to the full 902-928 MHz band is non-compliant in Brazil, and EU 865-868 MHz inlays read short. HF access cards at 13.56 MHz are globally harmonised and unaffected — specify the Brazilian tuning only for UHF inlay and label orders.

faq.question: Do your RFID products need ANATEL homologation?
faq.answer: ANATEL homologation is mandatory for radio-communication equipment before it is imported, sold or operated in Brazil, and it requires testing at ANATEL-accredited Brazilian laboratories — FCC or CE reports do not substitute. Only active, transmitting equipment is homologated, which is the reader/interrogator; passive RFID tags and inlays are field devices powered by the reader and are exempt. When evaluating a UHF system, ask your reader vendor for the ANATEL homologation number, and specify the passive tags by their band tuning (902-907.5 / 915-928 MHz) and air-interface standard.

faq.question: Can you supply RFID ear tags for cattle identification?
faq.answer: Yes. We manufacture both UHF and LF (134.2 kHz, ISO 11784/11785) RFID ear tags suitable for livestock identification programs. Our cattle ear tags are designed for long-term outdoor use with UV-resistant and waterproof construction. Brazil has the world's largest commercial cattle herd (over 200 million head), so contact our team with your specific requirements for Brazilian livestock traceability applications.

faq.question: How do import taxes and customs work when importing RFID to Brazil?
faq.answer: RFID cards and tags classify under NCM 8523.52 (the Mercosur nomenclature aligned to HS 8523.52). Brazil has no free trade agreement with China, so there is no tariff preference: Import Duty (II) applies on the CIF value, and IPI, PIS/COFINS and the state-level ICMS are layered on cumulatively, with the ICMS rate varying by destination state. The taxes are paid by the importer of record when the goods clear through SISCOMEX. We provide FOB and CIF pricing plus NCM guidance so your customs broker can calculate the landed cost accurately; the exact rates depend on the final NCM and your state, so confirm them with your broker. For large-volume orders, the total landed cost from Proud Tek is typically 30-50% lower than sourcing from domestic Brazilian distributors.

faq.question: What Incoterms can Brazilian buyers choose?
faq.answer: Brazilian buyers can order EXW Shenzhen, FOB Shenzhen/Yantian, or CIF to a Brazilian port such as Santos or Paranagua. Because Brazilian import taxes are paid by the importer of record when the goods clear via SISCOMEX, DDP-to-door is uncommon for RFID consumables — EXW/FOB/CIF with your own customs broker is the norm, and we support all three, with the NCM 8523.52 line and a certificate of origin on every invoice.

faq.question: Can I get product samples before placing a large order?
faq.answer: Yes. We provide free sample kits including RFID cards, tags, labels and wristbands shipped via express courier to any Brazilian address at no charge. For UHF orders the samples are tuned for the Brazilian sub-bands (902-907.5 / 915-928 MHz) so the test reflects Brazilian field conditions. Custom-printed samples with your artwork are also available.
